sheet.title: Case endings, decoded.
sheet.subtitle: A visual guide to **Waṣl** (linking) and **Waqf** (stopping) · Book pp. 109-114
sheet.coreIdea: You are **not choosing** the grammatical ending in these exercises. The ending is already written. You choose **how to pronounce it.**
sheet.coreIdeaNote: The rule is about reading and pausing, not about deciding whether the word should end in -u, -a or -i.

items.title: WAṢL / CONTINUE READING
items.caption: Read the written final vowel or tanween when the next word follows.
items.note: The first word links; you stop on the last word.

items.title: WAQF / STOP READING
items.caption: At the word where you pause, the ending becomes sukuun.
items.note: The written -un is not pronounced at the stop.

items.title: Decide
items.text: Continue to the next word, or pause?

items.title: Pronounce
items.text: Waṣl: read it. Waqf: convert it.

items.title: Exception 1 · Tanween fatḥah
items.note: Not on ة: حِكْمَةً -> ḥik mah (p. 115).

items.title: Exception 2 · Taaʔ marbuuṭah ة
items.note: Two dots = ة. Plain ه is /h/ either way: وَجْهٌ waj hun / wajh.

sheet.exerciseIntro: Follow the printed vowel marks. Don't invent new case endings.

exerciseTips.title: Locate
exerciseTips.text: the **last sign** on the printed word.

exerciseTips.title: Waṣl
exerciseTips.text: keep the ending in your pronunciation.

exerciseTips.title: Waqf
exerciseTips.text: use the conversion table on page 1.

exerciseGuide.task: Transcribe each word for both waqf and waṣl
exerciseGuide.method: Find the **last mark**. **Waṣl:** read it as written, tanween included. **Waqf:** make it sukuun; tanween fatḥah -> long **aa**; final ة -> **/h/**. The rest of the word, long vowels included, stays the same.

example.translit: ki taa ba tun / ki taa bah
example.note: Waṣl / waqf (No. 2) · final ة -> /h/ at the stop

contrast.note: Watch out (No. 5): tanween fatḥah on ة does **not** become long aa

exerciseGuide.task: Rewrite each sentence, then transcribe it as you would pronounce it
exerciseGuide.method: Link every word into the next (**waṣl**) and read all printed endings. Apply **waqf** only on the last word, or where you deliberately pause. Only the stopped word changes.

sheet.exerciseFooter: **Not yet taught in this chapter:** how grammar decides whether a word ends in -u, -a or -i. Chapter 5 supplies those marks and trains you to read them correctly when linking or stopping. **This is a pronunciation task, not a case-selection task.**

back.en: Linking: reading a word straight into the next one without a pause. The written ending is pronounced.
Stopping: pausing on a word, whether it is read alone, in the middle of a sentence or at the end.

front.en: At a stop, what do ḍammah, fatḥah, kasrah, tanween ḍammah and tanween kasrah become?

back.en: All of them become sukuun: the final vowel and the -n are not pronounced.

front.en: At a stop, what does tanween fatḥah become on a letter other than ة?

back.en: Alif: a long aa. ra ju lan -> ra ju laa. On ة, stop with /h/ instead: ḥik ma tan -> ḥik mah.

front.en: At a stop, what happens to a word that already ends in sukuun?

back.en: Nothing: it stays sukuun (ra jul -> ra jul).

front.en: Taaʔ marbuuṭah ة: how is it pronounced in waṣl and in waqf?

back.en: Waṣl: /t/ like a normal taaʔ. Waqf: /h/.

front.en: Which is the one case where waqf changes the sound of a letter itself, not just the ending?

back.en: Taaʔ marbuuṭah ة: /t/ becomes /h/ at the stop.

front.en: Taaʔ marbuuṭah (ة ـة) vs haaʔ (ه ـه): how do you tell them apart?

back.en: Look for the two dots: ة has them, ه does not.

front.en: At a stop, how do a word ending in ة and a word ending in ه sound?

back.en: The same: both end in /h/ (luʿ bah, wajh). Only in waṣl do they differ (/t/ vs /h/).

front.en: May you still pronounce the full ending when you stop?

back.en: Yes. That is how you read words so far, and many beginners do it to keep ة and ه apart. Applying waqf is more natural.

front.en: Where is the case ending in this word?

back.en: On the last letter only: the ḍammah on د. The marks before it are the word's ordinary harakaat.

front.en: A harakah inside اَلْمَلِكُ (the king) was changed. What happened?

back.en: It became a different word: the angel. Changing an inside harakah changes the word; the ending only changes how the word works in the sentence.
